name: Butbut Kalinga
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: There is a phoneme of stress. Intonation often makes it difficult to determine word stress because pitch is raised on the final syllable of a phrase. However, stress appears to be manifested by lengthening of the vowel when word stress is on an open penultimate syllable. [...] The clue may be that when the vowel in the penultimate is lengthened it receives the stress placement, since vowel length appears to occur only in stressed syllables; and when the penultimate is short, stress is on the final syllable. There is also secondary stress and there is length on the vowels of open syllables so stressed. Usually it appears that secondary stress is on the second syllable preceding primary stress, but sometimes it occurs three syllables before, particularly in verbs.

However, stress appears to be manifested by lengthening of the vowel when word stress is on an open penultimate syllable. Stress is difficult to determine otherwise, since the vowel of a closed penultimate and of both open and closed final syllables will not carry length even though word stress may be on one of these syllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Contrastive (phonemic) word stress of the usual Philippine type: primary stress falls on either the penult or the final syllable and is lexically fixed per word (minimal pairs 'ba:lat 'banana' vs ba'lat 'broth'; '?u:tut 'rat' vs ?u'tut 'flatulence'; man'su:gob 'to quarrel' vs manso'gob 'to burn'). A stressed open penult is long; otherwise (short penult) stress is final. Unstressed /a/ reduces to schwa.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Present: usually on the second syllable before the primary stress, sometimes three syllables before (especially in verbs); open syllables bearing secondary stress are lengthened.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is described as hard to determine except on an open penult (which is lengthened); vowels of closed penults and of final syllables carry no length even when stressed. Suffixation causes 'stress shift' (sec. 2, p. 98, e.g. da'kol 'big' -> da.ko'lan 'very big'). Butbut named as the chief divergent dialect, but only a segmental difference (b -> [h]) is cited.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonemic word stress, sec. 1.5); the author notes that phrase-final pitch raising (intonation) obscures word stress and that further study is needed. Examples are isolated citation forms. Note 1 (p. 99): data from Mallango barrio, Tinglayan, collected since 1974 -- Southern (Bangad) Kalinga [ksc], not Butbut proper.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is NOT for Butbut proper. Grayden 1979 describes 'Southern Kalinga' from Mallango barrio, Tinglayan municipality (note 1, p. 99), which is Southern/Bangad Kalinga [ksc] = Glottolog sout2908; the same note calls Butbut the 'chief dialectical difference' within that Southern Kalinga area (syllable-initial b -> [h]). Glottolog 5.1 attached this paper to butb1235, Glottolog 5.3 no longer does. Ethnologue (via Wikipedia) gives 82% lexical similarity Butbut-Southern Kalinga. If the catalog keeps the entry under butb1235 it should be flagged as a sister-lect (sout2908) description; otherwise file it under sout2908 and leave butb1235 as 'no first-hand statement'.

sources.citation: Ferreirinho, Naomi. 1993. Selected topics in the grammar of Limos Kalinga, the Philippines. Pacific Linguistics B-109. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Fullest modern grammar of any Kalinga lect (Limos, kmk); its phonology chapter would give the Kalinga-wide picture of contrastive stress against which the Butbut/Southern data can be read. Sister language, not Butbut.

sources.citation: Gieser, C. Richard. 1958. The phonemes of Kalinga. In Studies in Philippine Linguistics (Oceania Linguistic Monographs 3), 10-23. Sydney: University of Sydney. [Guinaang barrio, Lubuagan = Lubuagan Kalinga knb; Rosetta Project mislabels it kmd]
sources.note: Sec. 1: 'The suprasegmental phonemic contrast is in stress'; sec. 3.3: 'Stress has not been fully studied as yet; therefore, little more than its phonemic status can be declared at this point', with minimal pairs (bálat 'banana' / balát 'broth'). Sister language (Lubuagan Kalinga), not Butbut.

Scripture video / YouVersion / eBible links only; no dictionary or linguistic material listed.

Butbut page (from Ethnologue): villages Bugnay, Buscalan, Butbut Proper, Loccong, Ngibat (Tinglayan) plus Tabuk and Rizal sites; 82% lexical similarity with Southern Kalinga; 'nontonal'; no phonology. Kalinga page: Lubuagan Kalinga orthography note (Hohulin & Zamora 1995): 'An acute accent may be used on a stressed vowel to distinguish words.. but otherwise stress is not usually marked.'
